questions.q: Why would you raise your own error deliberately?
options: To signal a business rule violation that SQL Server itself wouldn't otherwise catch
SQL Server requires every script to raise at least one error
To disable TRY/CATCH for the rest of the script
It's the only way to run a SELECT statement
questions.explain: A rule like 'discount can't exceed 50%' isn't a syntax or constraint error SQL Server would catch on its own.

questions.q: What does THROW with no arguments do inside a CATCH block?
options: Raises a brand new, generic error
Re-raises the exact error that was just caught, unmodified
Suppresses the error entirely
Restarts the TRY block from the beginning
questions.explain: This is useful for logging or reacting to an error while still letting it propagate up to the caller.

questions.q: Which syntax is recommended for raising a custom error in new T-SQL code?
options: RAISERROR
Both are equally recommended with no preference
THROW
Neither — custom errors are not supported in T-SQL
questions.explain: RAISERROR predates THROW and is still common in existing code, but THROW is the modern, recommended choice for new development.

questions.q: What are the three arguments THROW takes when raising a new error?
options: THROW takes no arguments under any circumstances
An error number, a message, and a state
A table name, a column name, and a value
A severity level, a message, and a line number
questions.explain: THROW 50000, 'Product does not exist.', 1; shows this three-argument shape.

questions.q: What does RAISERROR's second argument (e.g. 16 in RAISERROR('...', 16, 1)) represent?
options: A column index
The error's line number
The number of times to retry
A severity level — 16 is a common 'user-caused' error severity
questions.explain: RAISERROR's argument shape (message, severity, state) differs from THROW's (error number, message, state).
